newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa's P.W. Botha breaks his silence -- a bit.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa's P.W. Botha breaks his silence -- a bit.

text.p: Former South African president P.W. Botha has broken the long silence of his angry retirement, but political analysts said on Friday he was unlikely to shed much light on the true history of his decade in power.

The reclusive Botha, claiming innocence of the horrors of apartheid, served "truth commission" chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu tea and snacks on Thursday but offered little to further South Africa's probe into human rights abuses under white rule.

In his most extensive public statement since he was ousted in a cabinet coup initiated by F. W. de Klerk in 1989, Botha insisted: "I am not guilty of any deed for which I should apologise or ask for amnesty."

Botha, now 80, presided over the most brutal phase of white rule during which more than 2,000 people were slain by police, women and children were tortured, thousands were jailed without trial and the black majority was subjected to years of grinding emergency rule that cancelled most of their few rights.

Blaming the atrocities of apartheid on "individuals (who) exceeded the limits of their authority", Botha told Tutu: "As a Christian and an Afrikaner, I cannot and have never associated myself with blatant murder."

Tutu, who has subpoenaed reluctant police, army and cabinet leaders of the apartheid era to appear before his statutory commission on human rights crimes in the war over apartheid, agreed to see Botha in his retirement town of Wilderness.
He later told reporters the two-hour meeting over herbal tea and sausage rolls was "a breakthrough" for his apartheid probe.
Arguing against black demands that Botha should answer in public for the actions of his government, Tutu said he should be accorded the respect of a former head of state.
Analysts doubted much would come of Botha's cooperation.

"What comes across most clearly is that Botha has not changed his position at all. If he is saying he is willing to cooperate, you can be sure it will be on his own terms," said University of Cape Town political scientist Andre du Toit.

He said Botha's denial of responsibility for the horrors of apartheid could be undermined by the testimony of former agents of white rule, including veteran police chief Johan van der Merwe and former law and order minister Adriaan Vlok.
"These men have said they will apply for amnesty and that means they must make full disclosure of what they did. These are not men who will make their allegations lightly.
"I don't think that at this stage P.W. Botha can just deny everything and expect to get away with it," du Toit said.

Stellenbosch University political analyst Willie Breytenbach was impressed that Botha had agreed to see Tutu, whereas he refused to see de Klerk. But he said there was no sign that Botha would disclose anything new in future.
"Clearly, Archbishop Tutu wants to avoid subjecting Botha to a public grilling. I don't understand why and I don't think it's going to go down well with the black population," he said.
Botha went further for Tutu, whose 1984 Nobel Peace Prize he has never acknowledged, than he did for de Klerk, his successor as leader of the Afrikaner-dominated National Party (NP).

De Klerk told the "truth commission" recently that Botha refused to help him draw up a submission on the NP's 47 years in power, in which he too denied blame for the killings, torture, detention and abuse of civil rights under apartheid.
For Tutu, Botha offered to facilitate private meetings with police, military and cabinet security chiefs who managed what he terms a crusade against "the onslaught of Soviet imperialism".
But in an apparent attempt to claim some of the credit usually given to de Klerk for dismantling apartheid, Botha said it was he who initiated the process of reform in 1984.
Amongst his achievements he listed the relaxation of restrictions on blacks at white universities, abolition of a ban on mixed sex and marriage and the desegregation of beaches.
"I personally initiated the process which eventually led to the release of President Nelson Mandela," he said -- a claim many South Africans would dispute.
